title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
hook: a string of beads in a coat pocket, one bead larger than the rest, and a rule about never crossing it

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana began with Arjuna's wind and Krishna's answer: practice, and a resolve that sets the terms. Did you write your four terms down? Day one thousand thirteen.

In a coat pocket, a loop of beads. Small wooden ones, or knobbly dark seeds, worn smooth by a thumb. One bead is larger than the others and sits apart, with a tassel hanging from it. Some who keep japa follow a rule about that big bead. You go all the way round the loop, bead by bead, and when you arrive back at it, you don't step over it. You turn the whole string around and go back the way you came. Why would a bead be something you don't cross? Today, the mala: the string of beads that goes with japa for some who keep it, and what it's doing in the hand.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN A POCKET.` → `ONE BEAD SITS APART.` → `YOU DON'T CROSS IT.`

segments.voice: The string is called a mala. The word means a garland, the kind of string of flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting. The beads vary by tradition. Tulsi wood is tied to devotion to Vishnu and Krishna. Rudraksha seeds, the knobbly dark ones, are tied to Shiva. The large bead is called the meru, the same name as the sacred mountain at the center of the world in Hindu cosmology. Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it, and the reasons they give vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru, or for God, and you don't step over what you honor. Others say turning back keeps the round from becoming mindless, a loop you could spin forever without noticing. Either way, the meru marks a boundary: a round has an end, and you know when you've reached it. Now look at the thread. In the Gita, chapter seven, Krishna says that all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see. The thread holding them together is hidden. Some who keep japa hold that verse in mind as the beads pass: each repetition separate, all of them strung on one thing. And then there's the thumb. In the Gita's sixth chapter, Krishna says that wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. A bead is a small, physical way of doing that. The mind drifts to a bill, a text message, a song. The thumb moves to the next bead. The bead is the coming back, made into something you can feel.
screen: `MALA: A GARLAND FOR COUNTING.` · `THE MERU: THE BEAD YOU DON'T CROSS.` · `GEMS STRUNG ON ONE THREAD.` · `EACH BEAD IS A COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. If you have a mala, hold it. If not, use your fingers: touch the thumb to each fingertip in turn. With each touch, say your mantra once, silently or in a whisper. Om will do, or a word from your own tradition. When the mind drifts, don't scold it. Just let the next touch be the coming back. When you reach the end of a round, pause, turn around, and go back the other way. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and each bead as a small return.
Your line: each bead a coming back. Today, once when your mind drifts in a queue or on a walk, press your thumb to a fingertip and count it as a bead: one coming back. Day one thousand thirteen.

howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: mala, a garland; a japa mala is a garland of beads for counting a mantra.

Confirm the meru customs (not crossing, turning back) and the reasons attributed to teachers; lineages differ.
